summary.text: A 13-year-old girl was evaluated at a psychiatric service for motor and vocal tics that had begun two years earlier and progressed in intensity. Tics included hand shaking, heel hitting, smiling during speech, coughing, throat clearing and repeating the letter "A". Past history included hyperactivity without treatment, a normal birth and normal neuromotor development and school performance.

One year after the first evaluation the tics intensified, hampering school performance and social relationships, and obscene tics and copropraxia emerged. She was initially treated with pimozide with only partial response, with elevated prolactin and akathisia, then switched to risperidone 3 mg/day with topiramate added; severity progressed rapidly and response was poor.

A secondary cause was suspected and a T2-weighted MRI showed bilateral hyperintensity in the medial globus pallidi, the "eye of the tiger" sign. Genetic testing confirmed a PANK 2 gene mutation and the diagnosis of PKAN, reported as an atypical case presenting with Tourettism.

Ten months after the diagnosis she developed choreic movements in the lower and upper limbs and athetosis in the right foot. Tic frequency reduced despite no change in treatment dosage, while emotional control worsened with tantrums, aggression and more severe hyperactivity, and school performance declined, hindering attendance.

ambiguities.issue: The article says the symptoms resembled typical Tourette syndrome ("apparent typical symptoms of TS") and the title says they did not match it; no Tourette syndrome diagnosis is stated as made or refuted for this patient, so no Tourette syndrome condition is recorded.

evidence.quote: This patient showed apparent typical symptoms of TS, but severity and lack of therapeutic response to typical TS medication led to further investigation with radiologic imaging.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not record Tourette syndrome as a confirmed or refuted diagnosis.

ambiguities.issue: The author hypothesis that basal ganglia dysfunction from iron accumulation promoted the Tourette-like symptoms is a hedged mechanism, not an established cause, and is not recorded as a fact.

evidence.quote: we hypothesized that dysfunction of basal ganglia circuitry caused by the iron accumulation may have promoted the manifestation of Tourette symptoms

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not assert iron accumulation as a measured or proven cause.

ambiguities.issue: The source does not say which treatment (pimozide, risperidone or topiramate) the "poor response to treatment" refers to, so the poor-response event is not ordered against the risperidone/topiramate switch; the order of the MRI and the genetic testing relative to each other is also not stated.

evidence.quote: Rapid severity progression and poor response to treatment led to the hypothesis of a secondary cause of the tics and an MRI was ordered.
Genetic testing confirmed mutation in the PANK 2 gene and the diagnosis of PKAN.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not attribute the poor response to a specific drug, and do not infer that the MRI preceded genetic testing from paragraph order.
